chapter_theme: Freedom from anger: the worthy let honour and insult pass alike, guard their tongues, bear harsh words from those beneath them and do not return harm, while their anger, when it comes, cools of itself. The base nurse and broadcast theirs.
structure_note: Most quatrains set the worthy (விழுமியோர், சான்றோர், மேன்மக்கள்) against the base (கீழ், நீசர், கயவர்): 64, 66, 68 and 70. 65, 66 and 69 ground restraint in power and lineage rather than weakness.

61.reading: Let those who honour us pass, and let those who trample us pass too; since even a fly can climb onto one's head, those who understand this do well to be free of burning anger.
61.nuance: The fly deflates the insult: being stepped on is something even the smallest creature does, so it carries no weight. The printed second and third lines repeat மதித்- where both commentators read மிதித்- (trample), and the last line's wording looks corrupt.

62.reading: Those whose minds can carry a task through will not throw away their precious life whenever they meet disgrace, even when it presses so hard they cannot move a step.
62.nuance: Placed in a chapter on not being angry, the quatrain can be read as treating death at humiliation as anger turned on oneself. That is an interpretation from its placement; the verse itself argues only from the unfinished task.

63.reading: Unguarded words from an open mouth burn the speaker without end, so the learned, who listen and reflect without end, never speak scorching words even when angry.
63.nuance: The repeated ஓவாதே sets the endless burning of careless speech against endless listening as its cure. The burn falls on the speaker, not the hearer.

64.reading: The excellent do not grow hot with anger when people beneath them confront them with unfit words; the base brood on it, rant for the town to hear, leap about and butt a pillar.
64.nuance: The comic last line makes anger self-injuring rather than wicked: the head that hits the pillar is the angry man's own.

65.reading: Restraint in youth is true restraint, a gift from one without wealth is the true fruit of giving, and the patience of a strong person able to punish everything is true patience.
65.nuance: Each virtue counts only where its opposite would be easy: youth tempts, poverty excuses, power permits.

66.reading: The well-born bear the stone-like bitter words of the base in front of everyone and let them pass, held back by their own lineage as a cobra's hood is quelled at once by sacred ash.
66.nuance: The image grants that the noble have venom: their forbearance is power held in, not its absence.

67.reading: The wise do not call it weakness to decline a fight with those who come at you as enemies; even when they confront you and do unbearable harm, it is good not to harm them in return.
67.nuance: The first half answers the charge of weakness before the second recommends restraint. With neither commentary aligned, this reading rests on the Tamil and Pope.

68.reading: The anger of the low keeps spreading however long it runs and never dies, while the anger of the worthy cools of itself, like the heat water takes on when boiled.
68.nuance: Water's heat is borrowed from the fire, so the simile can suggest that the worthy's anger comes from outside and leaves them as they were. That is my reading of the image, not the commentators'.

69.reading: Even when people forget the help they received and do great harm, those born in families whose fame touches the sky only keep doing good, and do not seek to repay the fault with harm.

70.reading: No one bitten by a raging dog bites it back; so when the low speak low words, will the high answer in kind with their own mouths?
70.nuance: The analogy works by ranking the insulter with the dog: answering in kind would mean stooping to its level.

links.note: Both find the model of bearing scorn in something below us: 151 in the earth that holds up those who dig it, 61 in the fly that climbs on one's head.

Kural 969 praises those who, like the yak, give up life when honour is lost. 62 says those set on finishing their work don't give up life whenever disgrace comes. Both answer whether disgrace is a reason to die. The conflict holds if 969's மானம் covers the humiliation 62 has in mind; 62 limits itself to those with a task to complete.
Both make speech a burn. In 129 the tongue's burn on the hearer never heals; in 63 careless words burn the speaker without end.
153 calls bearing with the ignorant the strength of strengths; 64 shows the excellent doing it and the base failing at it.
Both count restraint only where it costs something: 301 says one who checks anger where it could take effect truly checks it, and 65 that true patience belongs to one with the power to punish.
65 calls the gift of one without wealth the true gift; 91 promises open doors in the next world to those who give gladly even when they have little.
Both praise bearing the bitter words of those who overstep. 159 likens such people to renunciants in purity; 66 credits their lineage with the restraint.
Both make not returning harm to one who has harmed you the mark of the good. 67 adds that this is not weakness.
Both make the anger of the good brief. Kural 29, in Parimelazhagar's reading, adds that even while it lasts it can't be withstood; 68 stresses only that it cools of itself, leaving out its force.
987 asks what worth is for if it doesn't do good even to those who did harm; 69 says the well-born do exactly that, even to the ungrateful.

source_issues: 61: the Tamil prints மதித்திறப் பாரும் twice and மதித்தேறி where Mudaliar (மிதித்து) and Shanmuganar (மிதித்து நடப்பவரும், மிதித்து ஏறி) read மிதித்-; சுதமின்மை in the last line looks corrupt (Shanmuganar has சுடும் சினம்). Mudaliar's commentary breaks off after மிதித்து.
67: neither Mudaliar's nor Shanmuganar's commentary is aligned.
61-70: Shanmuganar's notes carry the numbers 121-130, from an edition that orders the chapters differently; the content matches these quatrains.
